Amended laws spur collective sale hopes, even as developers remain choosy
article:
Six weeks after Parliament passed a Bill on Sept 8 lowering the consent threshold for collective sales of older developments, at least 19 strata developments are exploring or preparing for en bloc sales.

Many are still in the early stages of the collective sale process, notes JLL. They range from those assessing the feasibility of a collective sale to those that have already appointed marketing agents.

These include privatised HUDC estates such as Braddell View and Lakeview Estate , commercial developments including The Arcade and Manhattan House , and mixed-use projects such as Upper Serangoon Shopping Centre .

However, the growing number of collective sale hopefuls has yet to translate into more deals. Whether it will “ultimately depends on realistic pricing from owners”, says Nicholas Ng, head of land and collective sales at JLL Singapore.

“From experience, large projects embarking on collective sales for the first time rarely succeed, as owners have not yet experienced failure and often maintain unrealistic price expectations,” he adds.

Developers remain selective, with only three significant collective sales recorded this year: Tan Boon Liat Building, which Kingsford Group agreed to purchase for $950 million in July; Loyang Valley, acquired by SingHaiyi Group for $880 million in April; and the rear block of The Centrepoint , purchased by Frasers Property for $391.9 million in February.

Among those preparing for another attempt is International Plaza , the 50-storey Tanjong Pagar landmark whose owners have formed a new collective sale committee (CSC). It will be the development’s second attempt, following an unsuccessful launch at $2.7 billion in 2021 — then the highest asking price for an en bloc sale.

Completed 50 years ago, International Plaza occupies a 75,089 sq ft site with 43 years remaining on its 99-year lease.

The new CSC is chaired by Gerald Cheong, executive director of Tian Teck Investment Holdings, which owns a substantial stake in International Plaza. Kevin Liang, who chaired the previous CSC, returns as secretary.

The committee has yet to set the reserve price, as it is “in the midst of appointing a marketing agent and a lawyer”, Liang says.

More sites, few takers

Tenders for 10 collective sale sites have recently closed, or are scheduled to close in October, with more to follow in November.

Several have attracted enquiries but no firm bids. For example, People’s Park Centre in Chinatown, launched for the third time at $1.48 billion, received no bids when its tender closed on Sept 16. The development is now in a 10-week private treaty period ending Nov 24.

“While there were no bids at the close of the tender, there were some enquiries,” says Sunny Wong, division director at ERA Realty, which is handling the sale.

City Plaza , a freehold mixed-use development in Paya Lebar Central, is also in private treaty after its third collective sale tender closed on Oct 13 without a bid. The guide price was $970 million.

Terence Lian, head of investment sales at Huttons Asia, says expressions of interest have been received.

Two residential developments marketed by JLL — Lakeside Towers in Jurong West and Gilstead Court in Newton — have likewise entered private treaty after their tenders closed on Oct 1 and Oct 13, respectively.

The 144-unit Lakeside Towers, on its third attempt, had a reserve price of $350 million, or $1,277 psf per plot ratio (ppr). The development has 48 years remaining on its lease.

Gilstead Court, a 48-unit freehold condo in prime District 11, is on its fourth attempt since 2008, with a reserve price of $198 million, or $1,874 psf ppr.

“Both Lakeside Towers and Gilstead Court attracted viewing activity during the marketing phase,” says Ng. Their private treaty periods end around Dec 9 and Dec 21, respectively.

High Point , a 59-unit freehold condo on Mount Elizabeth, is also in its private treaty period, which ends on Dec 21, after its sixth collective sale tender by ETC (a member of Realion Group) closed on Oct 12. The development had a guide price of $580 million.

Meanwhile, two developments relaunched for collective sale this month have tenders closing in November.

Balestier Regency , a 72-unit freehold development on Jalan Ampas, is making its fifth attempt at an unchanged guide price of $255 million. Its tender closes on Nov 12.

Beauty World Plaza , a 999-year leasehold mixed-use development next to Beauty World MRT Station, is on its third attempt at $165  million, with the tender closing on Nov 19.

Smaller sites, alternative uses widen buyer pool

While several larger collective sale sites have struggled to secure buyers, some smaller properties offering redevelopment flexibility have attracted stronger interest.

Pek Chuan Building on Lavender Street drew three bids when its third collective sale tender closed on Oct 7. GH15 Ventures, an investment vehicle of GH15 Investments, a company registered to operate hostels and dormitories, won with a bid of $80.68 million.

The successful bid was 4.8% above the $77 million asking price. It also exceeded the $80 million sought in the building’s two earlier attempts, in October 2025 and March 2026.

Terry Wong of Colliers Singapore represented the bidder, while Dillon Loi of Mount Everest Properties marketed the property.

The four-storey building can be redeveloped up to 12 storeys, while the buyer may also apply for a change of use to a hotel or mixed-use development. The property has about 51 years remaining on its lease.

Redevelopment flexibility is also generating interest in two freehold sites marketed by Knight Frank Singapore, whose tenders close on Oct 23.

One is Trendale Tower at 79 Cairnhill Road, which is on its fourth collective sale attempt.

Completed in 1982, the 20-storey freehold development comprises just 18 apartments on a 21,709 sq ft site. Its guide price of $168 million translates to $2,248 psf ppr, including the 7% bonus gross floor area (GFA) for balconies, according to Knight Frank.

The site could be redeveloped into a boutique luxury condo or a long-stay serviced apartment project. URA has indicated support for Serviced Apartment 2 (SA2) use under an outline planning permission application, subject to approvals.

Melvin Chay, interim head of capital markets at Knight Frank Singapore, says interest has been strong. “We have received a healthy mix of enquiries from developers exploring conventional residential redevelopment for sale, as well as investors with a longer-term investment horizon evaluating the potential for SA2 use for recurring income,” he says.

The two strategies have widened the pool of potential buyers beyond traditional residential developers, he adds.

Chay says developers have also identified a shortage of large-format apartments, which are in demand.

The other site, 154 Kampong Ampat, is a seven-storey industrial building in Tai Seng-MacPherson with a guide price of $105 million, or about $913 psf ppr.

Its existing GFA of 114,969 sq ft exceeds what its current zoning permits, while authorities have indicated support for workers’ dormitory use. The property has drawn enquiries from developers, dormitory investors and owner-occupiers, Knight Frank says.

In March, Soon Hock Enterprise, a developer and investor specialising in industrial assets, bought another industrial property, Kewalram House, for $120.51 million — $510,000 above its reserve price.

The pricing gap

Despite renewed interest in collective sales, developers remain cautious about acquiring en bloc sites, especially when Government Land Sale (GLS) sites offer a simpler alternative.

JLL’s Ng says developers have become “very selective”, partly because collective sale sites generally take longer to secure than GLS sites. “Many GLS sites benefit from proximity to MRT stations, which is a significant advantage given Singapore’s growing rail network connectivity,” he adds.

For owners, however, the motivation to pursue a collective sale rests largely on the premium they can secure over the resale value of their individual properties. Lee Liat Yeang, co-head of collective sales at Dentons Rodyk, says owners typically expect a “healthy premium”, particularly as those selling residential properties must also find replacement homes.

“This issue is particularly difficult if the owner is not a Singapore citizen or is a Singapore citizen with more than one residential property, given the potential additional buyer’s stamp duty (ABSD) exposure if they buy again,” adds Lee.

Over the past two decades, the premium from a collective sale has narrowed significantly. Ian Loh, managing director of Quinvest Chambers International Property Consultants, estimates the premium at 20% to 40% today, compared with 40% to 60% during the 2017 to 1H2018 en bloc wave, and 60% to 100% at the 2005–2006 peak.

Meanwhile, GLS land prices have continued to set new benchmarks. A site on Peck Hay Road fetched $1,865 psf ppr, a post-2018 high for the Core Central Region, while sites at Lorong Puntong and New Upper Changi Road set benchmarks of $1,612 and $1,537 psf ppr in the city fringe and suburbs respectively.

However, rising GLS prices are unlikely to drive developers towards collective sale sites, says Norman Ho, senior partner at Rajah & Tann Singapore.

En bloc acquisitions carry greater uncertainty, Ho continues, including potential objections from minority owners to the Strata Titles Board and delayed vacant possession, with owners generally allowed to remain up to six months after the sale is completed. GLS sites, by contrast, can be developed once they are awarded.

Higher GLS prices also push up the cost of replacement homes, making it harder for owners to agree on a reserve price, Ho notes.

He does not expect another wave of collective sales like the one nearly a decade ago. “A replacement home is also pricier, and the premium is much lower than before, so there is less incentive for them to sell and take the trouble to move out,” he says.

Owners who bought their units recently may also be reluctant to sell if doing so would trigger the seller’s stamp duty within the four-year holding period, JLL’s Ng adds.

Will lower consent thresholds make a difference?

The amendments to the Land Titles (Strata) Act are intended to make it easier for older developments to secure the majority consent needed for a collective sale.

Once the changes take effect, the consent threshold will fall from 80% to 70% for developments aged 40 to 59 years, and to 65% for those aged 60 years and above.

This could give some developments that previously struggled to secure sufficient consent another opportunity.

At Lagoon View, a 480-unit privatised HUDC estate in Marine Parade, the CSC had secured only 61% consent by end-August. The neighbouring 516-unit Laguna Park also failed to reach the 80% threshold in a recent attempt.

However, the amendments come with another significant change: CSCs will have just six months, instead of 12, to gather the required signatures. The waiting period after a failed collective sale attempt will also be extended from two years to three.

“Sometimes, owners take their own sweet time just because they have 12 months,” says Jeremy Lake, managing director of investment sales and capital markets at Savills Singapore.

“Now they will only have six months, so it will focus their attention, which is actually a good thing.”

However, Lake cautions that developments with 600 or more owners may struggle to secure the necessary consent within the shorter timeframe.

International Plaza is one such development. With 962 strata units comprising shops, offices and homes, securing 70% consent within six months could prove challenging. “It’s a large-scale mixed-use development,” says Liang, the CSC secretary.

Other large mixed-use developments are also looking to revive their collective sale ambitions.

Orchard Towers, launched at $1.6 billion in 2022, failed to secure a buyer, and a subsequent 2023 attempt fell short of the 80% consent threshold. Its owners are said to be restarting the process.

The owners of Far East Shopping Centre on Orchard Road are also said to be in the early stages of another collective sale attempt, following the collapse of a $908 million deal in 2024.

While lower consent thresholds may encourage more developments to pursue collective sales, securing a buyer remains a different challenge. “With ABSD, GFA harmonisation, rising redevelopment costs and other regulatory considerations, developers face tighter margins and greater financial risks,” says Quinvest’s Loh.

“Ultimately, easing the collective sale process does not necessarily translate into stronger developer demand or more successful en bloc transactions,” he adds.

title: Thomson Reserve draws over 23,000 visitors in first week of preview
article:
Thomson Reserve , the largest new private residential launch of 2026 with 1,268 units, has attracted more than 23,000 visitors in its first week of preview, ahead of its sales launch on Oct 31.

A spokesperson for joint developers UOL Group and CapitaLand Development says visitors have been predominantly Singaporeans and permanent residents, with interest coming from across the island.

Prospective buyers range from young couples and HDB upgraders to investors and larger families. Some families are considering purchasing multiple units within Thomson Reserve so that different generations can live close to one another, according to the developers.

There have also been enquiries from younger buyers who grew up in Upper Thomson and are now looking to establish their own homes in the familiar neighbourhood, says the developers.

The developers are seeing healthy interest in smaller units with efficient layouts and more affordable price quantum, while five-bedroom apartments appeal to larger families seeking more space and flexible layouts.

Marcus Chu, CEO of ERA Singapore, attributes the strong turnout to two factors: pricing and location.

After adjusting for strata area harmonisation, he says Thomson Reserve's indicative prices are comparable to resale prices at nearby JadeScape and AMO Residence .

Based on caveats lodged, recent resale transactions at JadeScape ranged from $2,292 to $2,710 psf in September and October, while those at AMO Residence ranged from $2,401 to $2,662 psf between June and September.

Thomson Reserve's indicative prices start from $2,608 psf.

Chu says the development's pricing is also in line with resale prices at newer condominiums near MRT stations across the Rest of Central Region (RCR).

"It's a rare chance to buy into a brand-new launch at resale prices," he says.

However, Chu believes location is the biggest draw. Thomson Reserve combines the appeal of an established residential enclave with proximity to Upper Thomson MRT Station, popular schools such as Ai Tong School, Thomson Plaza and surrounding greenery.

He likens the neighbourhood's appeal to that of Holland Village and Serangoon Gardens, with their mix of landed housing estates, shophouses and amenities.

The involvement of three established developers — UOL, SingLand and CapitaLand — also gives prospective buyers confidence in the quality of the development and its long-term value, he adds.

Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia, says Thomson Reserve's expansive site of over 5ha — equivalent to about seven football fields — mature location and wide range of apartment types appeal to both owner-occupiers and investors.

He notes particularly strong interest in three-bedroom units priced below $3 million, which he sees as a sweet spot for buyers in the current market. Larger units with four or more bedrooms have also attracted considerable interest, while smaller families and budget-conscious investors are looking at the two-bedroom units.

Kelvin Fong, CEO of PropNex, similarly expects the two-bedroom units, particularly the two-bedroom premium-plus-study layouts, to appeal to both owner-occupiers and investors.

He points to the strong rental performance of nearby JadeScape and AMO Residence as an indication of the area's investment appeal.

Based on URA rental data for 3Q2026, monthly rents for two-bedroom units at JadeScape ranged from $4,000 to $4,600, while three-bedroom units fetched between $5,600 and $7,600.

At AMO Residence, two-bedroom units commanded monthly rents of $3,200 to $4,600, while three-bedroom units fetched $4,800 to $5,700.

Located on the former Thomson View condominium site, Thomson Reserve comprises 1,268 units ranging from two- to five-bedroom apartments.

The development will continue its preview for a second week before bookings commence on Oct 31.

title: What's moving the market: Singapore's biggest property deals and hottest searches (Oct 23)
article:
Here is this week’s data-led look at Singapore’s property market, covering record transactions, rental benchmarks and the most searched homes on EdgeProp.

The following insights are compiled from EdgeProp Buddy , URA Realis and data.gov.sg, downloaded as of Oct 20.

Non-landed private homes — new launches, resales and rents

The priciest condo unit transacted in the past fortnight was a $10.8 million three-bedroom apartment at the luxury Parkview Eclat along Grange Road in prime District 10. The unit is situated on the 17th floor and measures 2,896 sq ft in floor area.

Parkview Eclat is an Art Deco-style, 35-unit, 21-storey condo designed by American architect James Adams, the same architect who designed Parkview Square , an office tower on North Bridge Road dubbed “Gotham City” for its striking architecture.

On the same street, freehold Grange Residences at 95 Grange Road made the list with the second highest-priced condo unit sold over the fortnight. A four-bedroom unit on Level 7 changed hands for $10.2 million or $3,576 psf.

The seller of the four-bedder made a profit of $2.9 million, going by caveat data compiled by EdgeProp Research. This is also the second-highest profit for the week among condo resales.

Meanwhile, the third most expensive condo unit transacted over the past 14 days was a five-bedroom unit at Gallop Green — a low-density, low-rise freehold condo along Woollerton Park off Farrer Road and near the Singapore Botanic Gardens.

The Gallop Green unit was sold for $9.4 million, which works out to $2,630 psf on its size of 3,574 sq ft.

New-launch projects with the highest transaction volumes in the fortnight to Oct 20 included Lucerne Grand along Lakeside Drive in Jurong, Union Square Residences on Havelock Road, as well as Coastal Cabana executive condo (EC) on Jalan Loyang Besar in Pasir Ris.

In the rental market, the most popular condos were The Sail @ Marina Bay with 49 rental deals and Marina One Residences with 45 deals, both in the Marina Bay district.

The rental yield averaged 4% at The Sail @ Marina Bay and 4.2% at Marina One Residences, based on URA rental data in the past 12 months.

Among condo units with the 10 highest rents, Ardmore Residence took up six spots. Apartments at the luxury 36-storey condo at 7 Ardmore Park, in District 10, are fetching monthly rents ranging from $29,200 ($9.27 psf) to $34,800 ($11.05 psf).

Landed homes — highest transacted prices and rents

In the landed property market, a detached house on Lim Tua Tow Road was sold for nearly $13.89 million on Oct 7, making it the highest-priced transaction over the fortnight to Oct 20. The price tag translates to $1,700 psf on its freehold land area of 8,170 sq ft.

On Faber Walk, a freehold semi-detached house sitting on a 7,334 sq ft site was resold for $12.75 million, garnering its owner a profit of $3.95 million. That works out to an annualised gain of 9.1% across a holding period of more than four years.

HDB flats — top prices and rents, most transacted blocks

A high-floor flat in Boon Keng was the priciest HDB resale deal in the last 14 days, at $1.64 million or $1,302 psf.

Following closely were two flats sold at nearly $1.59 million each — one at The Peak @ Toa Payoh , on Levels 31 to 33; and another at The Pinnacle@Duxton along Cantonment Road on Levels 28 to 30.

title: Sandy Tan’s Chalked broadens reach from showflats to private homes and the region
article:
Sandy Tan, founder of interior design firm Chalked, believes smaller spaces can still feel luxurious if the focus is on the quality of the finishes and on furniture proportioned to the space.

“It’s about creating a sense of refinement and balance, where every detail feels intentional without overwhelming the home,” she says.

Her showflat for Thomson Reserve , the 1,268-unit project at Bright Hill Drive, is a study in that balance. Tan imagined the owners of the 732 sq ft two-bedroom premium-plus-study unit as a young, active couple who love pickleball and music.

One bedroom became an audiophile's music room, the outline of a pickleball court runs across the ceiling, and pickleball paddles adorn the balcony. This year marks Tan’s third consecutive year as a judge of the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards, where her experience designing both showflats and private homes informs how she assesses projects.

From showflats to private homes

When Tan founded Chalked in 2017, 80% to 90% of its work involved designing showflats and sales galleries for developers, with only a handful of private homeowners as clients.

Today, about 60% of its residential projects are for private homeowners. “We have been getting a lot more of this work in the past two years,” says Tan.

She has since realised that private commissions make Chalked’s showflats better. “Engaging with homeowners gives us first-hand insights into how people actually live, what they value and how they use their spaces,” she says.

The firm is also winning over a growing number of high-net-worth homeowners. The key, says Tan, is understanding their lifestyles and respecting their privacy. “In this space, trust is everything.” Most new private clients come through word of mouth.

To Tan, luxury today lies less in extravagance than in craftsmanship and detail. “It’s the graceful curve of a handcrafted piece of furniture, the precision of a perfectly sewn stitch on a headboard, or heirlooms and collections that carry meaning,” she says.

Homeowners increasingly want spaces that reflect their lifestyle while expressing “a distinctly individual sense of self,” Tan notes.

What clients want

Even with most people back in the office, post-pandemic, clients still want a dedicated workspace at home.

Larger homes can accommodate a study, but in smaller ones, designers have to be creative, carving out a work area and concealing it within built-in cabinetry.

Chalked has applied the same thinking to developer projects, turning a flexible space of about 45 to 55 sq ft into a study in a compact showflat.

More are also asking for home automation. Smart home technology is now almost the norm, says Tan, with easy-to-use apps that work across a wide range of appliances.

“What was once a luxury has evolved into an affordable convenience for every home,” she adds.

She welcomes clients who arrive with Pinterest boards and AI-generated images of what they have in mind. “They make my job easier, not harder,” she says. They give the Chalked team a clear sense of a client’s taste, which the designers can then refine and test for feasibility.

Beyond homes

In recent years, Chalked has taken its approach to luxury into offices, shops and even a rehabilitation centre.

It designed Jung Asia’s Singapore headquarters, which officially opened earlier this month.

The German company specialises in high-end electrical switches, sockets and building automation systems for luxury homes, hotels and commercial spaces. It celebrated its 30th anniversary in Singapore at its new premises.

The headquarters is as much an experience centre as an office, and Jung Asia wanted it to showcase its heritage and quality, says Tan.

Besides the usual furniture and fittings, Chalked had to fabricate larger-than-life artistic sculptures for the space. “A lot of hard work went into the project,” she says.

Last year, Chalked designed Golden Seed Tea Café and Store at Millenia Walk , which bills itself as “a premium tea atelier” for Chinese tea.

The café recently won a regional design award for retail space.

The firm also designed The Winslow, a newly opened private residential addiction treatment centre licensed by the Ministry of Health.

Set in a heritage building at Hendon Road, in the Changi area, it is designed to feel like an upscale private residence.

“It was a unique opportunity to design within a regulated healthcare framework, balancing medical requirements with the safety, comfort and well-being of patients undergoing rehabilitation,” says Tan.

Following developers overseas

Chalked’s regional expansion has largely been driven by Singapore developers. The firm has worked on projects in Chengdu with Hong Leong Holdings and in Chongqing with GuocoLand. It is currently designing two show suites in Hai Phong, Vietnam, for CapitaLand.

Private clients are following the same path. Chalked recently completed a home in Discovery Bay, Hong Kong, for friends Tan first met in Singapore.

Additionally, some of its regular Singapore clients have asked the firm to design their homes in China.

In Singapore, Chalked continues to design showflats, and its work will be showcased in some of the upcoming launches.

Tan has kept her team lean: six people in Singapore, three in the Philippines and one in Malaysia. “We also have a strong collaboration with a firm in China that helps us with drafting,” she says. “I outsource more so we can keep our local costs as low as possible.”

She adds: “As our network of trusted and reliable vendors in the region continues to grow, we’re gaining greater confidence in taking on more projects across the region.”

title: HDB resale transactions jump 19.5% q-o-q in 3Q2026 amid policy changes
article:
Singapore’s public housing market saw a sharp increase in HDB resale transaction volumes in the third quarter of 2026. According to the Oct 23 HDB data release, 7,645 resale flats were transacted in 3Q2026, increasing on both a y-o-y and q-o-q basis.

The HDB resale market in the latest quarter was “largely shaped by policy shifts, seasonal trends and the absence of Build-To-Order (BTO) launches”, said Lee Sze Teck, senior director of data analytics of Huttons Asia.

The number of resale transactions rose by 19.5% in the latest quarter from 6,396 in 2Q2025, marking the highest volume of flats sold since 2024.

This was supported by a jump in the number of five-room and larger flats sold during the quarter, following the removal of the 15-month wait-out period for private property owners (PPOs) and ex-PPOs buying a non-subsidised resale flat in July, added Lee.

A total of 1,867 five-room flats and 545 executive and multi-generation flats were transacted in 3Q2026, spiking 26.7% q-o-q and 41.6%, respectively.

HDB resale transactions by flat type, 3Q2026

The five most popular HDB towns were Punggol, Sengkang, Tampines, Woodlands and Yishun. They accounted for around 36.6% of total transactions during the quarter.

Resale prices dip marginally

Meanwhile, HDB data showed that resale prices slipped for a third consecutive quarter, albeit at a moderate pace.

The resale price index inched down 0.1% q-o-q in 3Q2026, easing from the 0.3% fall logged in 2Q2025.

The third quarter saw nine out of 26 HDB towns recording price falls. The Central Area saw the largest decline of 8.4%, followed closely by Ang Mo Kio (-4.7%) and Jurong East (-4.3%).

Huttons’ Lee said: “While there was considerably more demand in the five-room and larger flats segment in 3Q2026, the impact on prices was relatively subdued.”

Mohan Sandrasegeran, head of research and data analytics at SRI, noted that the moderation in resale prices does not reflect a “broad-based weakening in buyer interest”.

Instead, it suggests a gradual translation towards a more balanced environment, coming on the back of several years of sustained price growth.

“While demand for resale flats remains relatively healthy, buyers appear to be exercising greater consideration over pricing, particularly as more housing options become available across the resale and new flat markets,” said Sandrasegeran.

Million-dollar flat sales hit record high

More buyers were willing to pay top dollar for resale HDB flats as million-dollar flat transactions reached a quarterly high of 596 in 3Q2026. That is the first time it has surpassed 500 transactions, marking an 21.6% q-o-q increase from the 490 units that changed hands in 2Q2026.

Resale HDB flat transactions priced at $1 million and above

Eugene Lim, key executive officer of ERA Singapore, observed that around 50.2% of million-dollar transactions in 3Q2026 involved resale flats aged 15 years or less, accounting for 299 deals.

“Younger flats have been a mainstay of million-dollar deals, as their new condition and longer remaining leases offer greater appeal,” Lim commented.

During the latest quarter, 26 transactions involved flats transacting above the $1.5 million threshold.

These transactions were concentrated in towns such as Queenstown, Bishan, the Central Area, Clementi, and Toa Payoh, according to Realion (OrangeTee & ETC) Group.

Resale market to face headwinds

Huttons’ Lee anticipates that the HDB resale market may bottom out in the last quarter of the year.

He pointed to the upcoming November 2026 BTO sales exercise, which will offer 7,690 new flats in sought-after locations such as Bayshore and Toa Payoh, as a factor that could temper resale activity.

Christine Sun, chief researcher and strategist at Realion Group, anticipates that the higher income ceiling for BTO flats following recent policy changes could divert demand away from larger, higher-priced resale flats.

Against this backdrop, Realion has revised its forecast for HDB resale price growth to 0% to 2% for the full year of 2026.

Despite this, SRI’s Sandrasegeran said that the resale market could observe a more “balanced distribution of demand” between the new and resale flat markets.

“Nevertheless, resale flats are expected to remain attractive to buyers with more immediate housing requirements, as well as thse prioritising specific locations, larger living spaces, or established neighborhood amenities,” he said.

SRI expects resale transaction volumes to total about 26,000 to 27,000 flats in 2026, with full-year price movements expected to come in between -1% to 1%.

title: Private home prices up 1.4% while rents gain 1.3% in 3Q2026, speeding up slightly
article:
Prices of private homes — excluding executive condos (ECs) — in Singapore increased by 1.4% q-o-q in the third quarter of this year, as compared with 0.5% in the preceding quarter, with landed homes leading the increase.

Rents likewise grew at a slightly faster rate, rising 1.3% q-o-q in the latest three months, up from 0.7% previously.

That is according to URA’s quarterly real estate statistics released on Oct 23, and is in line with its flash estimates published earlier in the month.

For the first nine months of this year, prices of Singapore’s overall private residential property price index increased by an average of 0.9% per quarter — similar to the corresponding period last year.

Landed homes got 2.9% pricier in 3Q2026, speeding up from the 2.5% increase in the previous quarter.

Meanwhile, prices of non-landed residential properties islandwide gained 1%, reversing from the 0.1% decrease in the previous quarter.

By region, the biggest percentage increase for non-landed homes came from the Outside Central Region (OCR) or suburbs at 2.3%.

This was followed by the Core Central Region (CCR) with a 0.3% rise, slowing from 1.8% in the previous quarter.

In the Rest of Central Region (RCR) or city fringe, prices of non-landed properties were unchanged in the third quarter, after a decrease of 1.2% in the second quarter.

Quieter new launch calendar

The stronger price growth coincided with a relatively quieter new-launch environment, as well as a shift in the mix of new home transactions towards higher price brackets, according to SRI head of research and data analytics, Mohan Sandrasegeran.

In the primary market, homes priced between $2 million and below $5 million made up some 68.2% of new private home sales during the third quarter, a bigger proportion than the 49.2% in the previous quarter.

This does not necessarily indicate that buyers are becoming less price-sensitive, as it may instead reflect the types of units available for purchase during the quarter, Sandrasegaran noted.

It also highlights how private residential price movements are influenced by a combination of factors, including the composition of transactions, the relative performance of different market segments and prevailing demand for residential properties.

"As such, the stronger price growth should not necessarily be interpreted as a broad acceleration across all developments, but rather as an indication of continued resilience in the overall private residential market," Sandrasegeran added.

Lull in sales activity

Meanwhile, the total number of private home transactions fell 16.3% q-o-q to 5,146 units — the lowest volume observed since 2Q2025.

The decline came amid lower launch volumes and homebuyer activity due to seasonal factors, ERA noted.

Resale transactions dipped from 3,813 in the second quarter to 3,801. They also accounted for 73.9% of all sales transactions this quarter, up from 62% previously, possibly due to the leaner pipeline of new launches, said Marcus Chu, chief executive of ERA Singapore.

He added that 52.4% of resales during the quarter involved OCR condos, which suggests "resilient demand from owner-occupiers and genuine demand for homes".

Riverfront Residences along Hougang Avenue 7 saw the most activity with 33 transactions, going by caveats lodged for resale condos during the quarter.

Next were D'Nest in Pasir Ris with 29 deals, while Normanton Park in District 5 and Treasure At Tampines tied for third place with 27 each, according to ERA.

Huttons Asia chief executive Mark Yip said that buyers leveraged on the slightly softer demand to negotiate for better prices, resulting in prices in the resale market easing by 1.1% in the third quarter.

Among new-launch projects, Lentor Gardens Residences was the best seller in the quarter, as buyers “were convinced of the transformation of the Lentor precinct, aided by the completion of Lentor Mall”, as well as its attractive pricing and the area’s investment viability, Yip opined.

Landed homes: Sustained buyer demand

A total of 588 landed homes were sold during 3Q2026, which is the highest quarterly volume for the segment so far this year.

This occurred even as the overall private housing market was less active.

ERA said the 2.9% q-o-q increase in landed home prices, up from the 2.5% growth in the previous quarter, could be attributed to more houses fetching at least $5 million, with the number rising to 308 in the latest quarter.

Notably, about 40.4% of landed homes sold for $5 million to $7.5 million, accounting for most of the quarter’s transactions.

"Landed homes continue to attract buyers for their long-term value and established appeal," Chu said.

Executive condo prices ease

The EC segment faced a shift in buyer behavior given the policy tightening in May this year.

The new EC rules encouraged some purchasers to opt for available inventory instead of waiting for upcoming launches, according to Huttons. As a result, developers sold 68 units from existing EC projects in 3Q2026.

Coastal Cabana moved 49 units at a median price of $1,829 psf, and Rivelle Tampines sold 18 units at a median of $1,938 psf.

The median price of ECs dropped by 1.6% q-o-q to $1,850 psf, down from $1,880 psf in the second quarter.

There were fewer than 150 unsold EC units in the market as of end-September 2026.

Rents of suburban condos see biggest increase

In the rental market, landed properties saw rents growing by 2.1% q-o-q, moderating slightly from the 2.7% increase in the previous quarter.

Among non-landed properties, rents were up 1.2%, accelerating from the 0.4% gain previously.

The OCR took the lead with a 3.1% jump in rents of condos and apartments, in contrast to the 0.3% decrease in the second quarter.

Next was the RCR with rents moving up by 1.5% for non-landed homes, after staying flat previously.

Moving in the opposite direction was the CCR, where rents of non-landed properties slipped by 0.3%, versus the increase of 1.2% in the preceding quarter.

Despite the overall 1.3% increase in islandwide rents, occupancy rates remained “healthy” at 92.8%, said Christine Sun, chief researcher and strategist of Realion (OrangeTee & ETC) Group.

Still, a surge in completed private residential stock — increasing by 3,491 units during the third quarter — led to overall vacancy rising to 7.2%, from 6.4% previously.

"AI has reshaped the employment landscape, potentially displacing some workers, while creating new roles and attracting AI-related businesses and talent to Singapore," Sun said. "Hence, landlords may need to adapt to changing tenant demographics, income levels and housing preferences."

Upcoming supply and outlook

A significant supply of about 32,800 private housing units, including EC units, could be made available for sale over the next one to two years, URA said on Oct 23.

This is part of the total supply of 57,200 private residential units expected to be completed over the next few years, and comes amid the large supply injection via government land sales (GLS).

In the second half of 2026, the government is launching GLS sites that can yield a total of 4,745 new private homes under the Confirmed List. That will bring the full-year GLS Confirmed List supply to 9,320 units, more than 50% above the annual average over the past decade, URA said.

Realion's Sun noted that the final quarter of this year will likely see a surge in transactions of private homes due to the highly anticipated line-up of several blockbuster launches, including Lucerne Grand , Thomson Reserve and The Serra Residences .

In particular, with 1,268 units and an average launch price of above $2,600 psf, Thomson Reserve in the RCR could lift the overall private property price index in the fourth quarter, Sun continued.

"Nevertheless, some buyers may exercise caution as interest rates could continue to rise in the months ahead," she said.

For the whole of 2026, Realion expects overall prices of private homes in Singapore to grow by 3–4%.

Yip from Huttons projected that total sales volume for the year could reach about 7,000 units, barring major market disruptions.

He added that this will be a "notable shift", as developer sales are set to outpace total new launches for the first time since 2022, which signals sustained demand for new private homes.

title: AI data centre backlash threatens Australia’s US$70 bil dream
article:
(Oct 23): More than three-quarters of data centres set to be built around Australia’s biggest cities are at risk from stretched power grids and local opposition, threatening the country’s ambition to become an artificial intelligence (AI) hub for the Asia Pacific region.

Of the 40-plus large centres planned or under construction in Sydney and Melbourne — representing more than A$100 billion (US$70 billion or $90 billion) of projected investment — just 23% have confirmed publicly that they have secured electricity supply or grid connections, according to a Bloomberg review of company disclosure. Those agreements, a gauge of whether or not a project is advancing, suggest significant setbacks and potential delays.

Australia has bet heavily on a data-centre boom that is intended to capitalise on its vast open spaces as well as clean-energy potential. To date, though, most of the project pipeline is clustered around Sydney and Melbourne — where almost two in five of its inhabitants live — in order to harness existing fiber networks and reliable power. Those operations put more strain on already stretched infrastructure, and leave developers on a collision course with residents.

In Sydney, seven of 28 active projects have confirmed power, according to Bloomberg’s analysis. In Melbourne, the figure drops to three out of 15.

Bloomberg contacted 25 developers to verify public disclosure on power supply and the status of more than 40 projects. Operator GreenSquare declined to comment on its power arrangements but said it was “working closely with relevant authorities and infrastructure partners to support long-term operational performance”. CDC Data Centres said it had “robust delivery plans in place for all sites currently under construction” with power delivery timelines as anticipated.

See also: SK data centre arm in talks to fund US$350 bil AI buildout in South Korea

Nine others declined to comment or didn’t directly answer queries on future projects. The rest did not respond.

The consequences of friction and delays are already apparent. Operator Nextdc Ltd slashed its profit forecast this week after Melbourne residents blocked the installation of towering transmission lines, almost halving the value of its shares.

In Sydney, Goodman Group abandoned its A$1.2 billion Project Mars development last month. The proposed 90-megawatt facility would have been built about 20 metres from the nearest home and 160 metres from a public school, prompting hundreds of objections to be submitted during the planning process.

See also: SoftBank's market value halves from peak as AI fears grow

“The social licence for Australian data centres is becoming an increasingly significant headwind,” Morgans Financial Ltd analyst Nick Harris wrote this week. “Investors are becoming concerned more delays could occur and question what the knock-on effect might be.”

The gulf between announced projects and those that will be built is also beginning to emerge in official data. Over a third of proposed data centres that would tap Australia’s main grid were cancelled last year, according to the Australian Energy Market Operator.

Part of the issue is the sheer scale of the build out. The country has more than 20 gigawatts of capacity in announced and early-stage data centre projects compared to an operational fleet of just 1.5 gigawatts, according to BloombergNEF.

“Access to energy is already a major issue,” said BNEF analyst Tushna Mehta. “Data centre capacity is being built much faster than the new generation needed to supply it.”

These hurdles are raising questions about the government’s push to make Australia a hub for the wider region, courting investors and seeking to streamline approvals even as practical constraints remain. Land may be plentiful, but data centres need access to high-voltage electricity lines and other infrastructure. Building further from the major cities can have advantages, but also means hefty investment in new transmission lines and telecommunications.

Sydney’s electricity grid is already struggling to accommodate the scale of the boom. Transgrid, which operates the statewide power network, said in August the city doesn’t have enough transmission capacity to connect any of the 20 gigawatts of inquiries it’s received from large new power users.

Half of that proposed demand has emerged within a 12km radius of its Sydney West substation, Transgrid said — equivalent to the peak winter electricity load of the entire state of New South Wales, in one small area.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

That strain is expected to intensify, and quickly. Australia already has more than 160 operating data centres, concentrated mainly in Sydney and Melbourne, which consume about 2% of electricity supplied by the country’s grids. AEMO has projected this could rise by a quarter each year to roughly 6% by 2030, and 13% by 2036.

Another hurdle is access to water. Industry-commissioned analysis estimates Australian data centres use about 5.5 gigalitres of water each year, largely for cooling — equivalent to roughly 0.04% of national consumption. But the local impact could be far greater when projects are clustered together, including in growth corridors already facing stress from drought.

Residents living near Nextdc’s facility in Melbourne’s West Footscray — about 15 metres from it, in some cases — told a parliamentary inquiry last month they wanted compensation for noise, pollution and potential fire risks.

“What we are seeing is rising public resistance to AI, particularly generative AI,” said Bronwyn Cumbo, who researches data centres at the University of Technology Sydney. “Many are planned to be built near homes, schools, farmland and natural areas, and alter the experience and livability of these places.”

title: Nippon Steel raises US mill upgrade to US$3 bil as costs climb
article:
(Oct 23): Nippon Steel Corp will spend US$3 billion building a hot-strip mill in Pennsylvania, part of its US$11 billion investment plan in newly-acquired US Steel.

The project will replace outdated facilities at the Edgar Thomson plant at the Mon Valley Works, Japan’s largest steelmaker said in a statement on Friday. The investment will increase annual production capacity from around 2.2 million tons to 3.5 million tons, with commercial operations expected to begin in the second half of 2029.

US Steel had said in June that investments to upgrade Mon Valley could total as much as US$2.5 billion. The jump reflects rising materials prices and a more accurate assessment of the project’s costs, said a spokesperson for Nippon Steel.

US Steel has become increasingly important to the Japanese firm after being acquired last year. In August, Nippon Steel raised its profit outlook for its American unit in the 2026 financial year by 80% from an initial forecast in May, reflecting a stronger US market.

“US Steel has become the key earnings driver of our group,” chief financial officer Takahiko Iwai said at the time.

The investment plan helped seal approval for the acquisition after an increasingly politicised review process that drew scrutiny from the White House.

title: China's US$150 bil AI model stock slump shows no sign of easing
article:
(Oct 23): There’s no end in sight for the sell-off in China’s artificial intelligence (AI) model developer stocks, with competition growing ever more heated and the threat of rival listings next year.

MiniMax Group Inc and Z.AI Co, also known as Zhipu, have shed a combined US$150 billion ($192 billion) in market value from their respective highs. The slide marks a brutal reversal after the duo’s hotly anticipated market debuts in January.

Domestic AI firms continue to slash token prices, while global giants Anthropic PBC and OpenAI have followed suit in order to minimise Chinese models’ cost advantage. Meanwhile, potential initial public offerings (IPOs) by DeepSeek and Moonshot AI could divert investor cash away from MiniMax and Zhipu, the only listed Chinese pure plays.

“Zhipu and MiniMax need to figure out how to win in the long term,” said Leonid Mironov, a portfolio manager at Gavekal Capital. “Between US models being better, and DeepSeek being most efficient, it’s hard to pinpoint exactly where MiniMax and Zhipu could go.”

MiniMax slid below its IPO price on Thursday, wiping out what had been a gain of 650% at its March peak. Larger peer Z.AI has tumbled 81% from its June high.

See also: China said to tighten scrutiny of listed company spinoffs — Bloomberg

The new M3.1 Flash model released by MiniMax on Monday provided no lift for its stock, despite sharply reduced token costs and improved performance. Zhipu has seen a similarly cold reaction to the launch of its GLM-5.3-FlashX in September.

According to the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, the pair’s latest offerings are far behind models from the US leaders in terms of intelligence. They even slightly trail DeepSeek, Alibaba Group Holding Ltd and Xiaomi Corp amid the continued flood of new products vying for usership.

“China currently has more than 10 AI labs, but eventually will be consolidating to less than that,” said Alex Liu, an analyst at Bank of America Corp. “Right now it’s actually hard to say who’s going to survive or who’s going to be the first to drop off.”

See also: Taiwan’s US$5 tril stock market to close on Friday as Typhoon Champi nears

On the plus side, Chinese models continue to dominate global usership. DeepSeek and MiniMax have officially completed registration for open-source releases and overseas use, a CCTV-affiliated WeChat account reported late on Thursday.

MiniMax already gets most of its revenue from outside of China, while Zhipu’s application programming interface (API) is gaining traction with global developers, JPMorgan Chase & Co strategists including Chloe Liu wrote in a note this week. The bank is bullish on Z.AI over MiniMax, seeing the former better positioned due to its coding capability.

The pair are still unprofitable, however, and global price wars make the bottom line outlook even tougher.

“Labs that lead on capability and paid API growth break even earlier than peers,” JPMorgan’s Liu wrote. AI models and applications should turn profitable “around 2028”, though the market remains focused on revenue mix for now, she added.

In addition to worries over competition, profitability and new Chinese AI stock offerings, Zhipu and MiniMax may also see pressure from looming share lock-up expiries. About 178 million Z.AI shares and 25 million MiniMax shares held by pre-IPO investors are due to become eligible for trading in January, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

title: SK data centre arm in talks to fund US$350 bil AI buildout in South Korea
article:
(Oct 23): SK Hyper Co is in talks with big tech firms and financial investors to secure funding for an envisioned US$350 billion ($447 billion) data centre buildout, joining a global rush to roll out artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure despite concerns about future demand.

The SK Group’s fledgling data centre arm has begun discussions with potential partners to help finance a plan to build 15 gigawatts of data centre capacity in South Korea by 2035, said Chung Suk-geun, SK Hyper’s chief executive officer. The first five-gigawatt phase alone would require US$350 billion including equipment, he told Bloomberg Television.

The company aims to secure its first round of external capital by the end of this year or early 2027, followed by further fundraising over the next three to four years. SK plans to share the overall cost with data centre tenants and outside investors, he added.

“We are under discussions with many strategic and financial partners,” Chung said in an interview. “We want to be prepared for meeting the market demand by making data centres in Korea.”

SK is pursuing an ambitious blueprint at a time markets are gyrating on fears of an AI bubble. Investors funding data centre projects are getting nervous that spending on future AI services won’t be enough to justify the trillions of dollars flowing into a global computing buildout.

Chung said his company would adjust the pace of investment according to actual demand, rather than commit to the entire plan upfront. “We are going to manage our risk appropriately, meeting with market demand,” he added.

See also: SoftBank's market value halves from peak as AI fears grow

Established in July as a unit of SK Telecom Co, SK Hyper is seeking to attract global technology companies to South Korea as a base for AI training and operations, serving Asian markets such as Japan and Taiwan rather than relying solely on domestic demand.

SK Group has plenty of affiliates — with expertise in chips, energy and telecommunications — that should help offset relatively high electricity costs by improving computing efficiency, Chung said. SK Telecom itself plans to invest 750 billion won (US$567 million or $723 million) in SK Hyper by 2030.

SK Hyper is developing a 900-megawatt project in the southern industrial city of Ulsan, alongside a previously announced 100-megawatt project for Amazon Web Services. It is in talks with the government to secure additional sites, Chung said.

See also: Red Hat opens Apac AI Centre of Excellence in Singapore, signs DSTA pact

It is also exploring opportunities to serve governments in Asia and the Middle East, offering computing capacity and AI models as an integrated package. Chung said SK Hyper could begin generating revenue as early as next year, ahead of the planned completion of its initial data centres in 2029.

title: China said to tighten scrutiny of listed company spinoffs — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 23): China is tightening scrutiny of publicly traded companies spinning off units for separate listings, according to people familiar with the matter, potentially putting the brakes on an important source of new deals.

The securities regulator has indicated it’s seeking to discourage firms from spinning off their most profitable parts for separate listings, which can be seen as unfair to the parent company’s shareholders, the people said. It also wants to ensure that any spun-off units operate in a different area than the parent, to reduce business overlap and related-party transactions, according to the people.

Regulators have started scrutinising applications for spinoffs in the mainland Chinese and Hong Kong stock markets more carefully, the people said. They could introduce more formal guidelines as early as next year, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.

Some companies have already shifted plans, including GoerTek Inc, which this month shelved a spinoff and listing of its microelectronics unit in Hong Kong. Yantai Dongcheng Pharmaceutical Co also dropped a plan to take a subsidiary public in Hong Kong, while Zhejiang Shuanghuan Driveline Co halted a plan to debut its robotics division on China’s A-share market in September.

The tightening comes amid rising investor concerns and market volatility, particularly in sectors related to artificial intelligence, in which China plays a critical role. Some other countries including South Korea have also been tightening scrutiny on spinoffs, with SK Hynix Inc this week scrapping plans for a potential US$10 billion US listing of its Solidigm unit after regulatory opposition.

Deliberations are ongoing and details of the Chinese regulator’s plans could change, the people said. The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) didn’t respond to a request for comment.

See also: Taiwan’s US$5 tril stock market to close on Friday as Typhoon Champi nears

Several other deals are still in the pipeline for now. They include Zhejiang Medicine Co’s biotech unit NovoCodex Biopharmaceuticals Co and Shandong Gold Mining Co’s overseas subsidiary Shanjin International Gold Co. Both are still awaiting approval. Baidu Inc’s chip unit Kunlunxin has also been planning an IPO in Shanghai, as well as Hong Kong.

In July, state-owned China Resources Power Holdings Co completed the separate listing of subsidiary China Resources New Energy Holdings Co in Shenzhen in one of the year’s largest A-share debuts. Shortly after, Hisense Group spun off its optical module unit, Ligent Technologies Inc, on the Hong Kong exchange.

Rules set in 2022 for spinoffs require the parent company to have been listed and profitable for at least three years, as well as capping the subsidiary’s contribution to its parent’s overall net profit and assets. The CSRC issued further guidelines a couple years later aimed at strengthening oversight and dissuading companies from tapping into unsustainable market hype for a quick cash fix.

title: UK set to ease up on senior bankers in bid to save firms £2 bil
article:
(Oct 23): UK regulators plan to spare 139,000 bank executives from yearly checks under the senior managers and certification regime in an effort to spur growth and save firms almost £2 billion (US$2.7 billion or $3.4 billion) over a decade.

Staffers below senior manager level will no longer be subject to annual certification or appear on the financial services register, the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) said in proposals published on Thursday.

The reforms — the first big changes proposed under new PRA head Katharine Braddick — would also end the requirement for regulators to pre-approve chief actuaries and chairs of risk and audit committees, instead asking firms to notify regulators of these appointments.

Senior staff including chief executive officers, chief financial officers and chairs will still require regulatory pre-approval, including fit and proper tests. The wider conduct rules, which cover about 900,000 people, are not changing, though the regulators plan to simplify training and breach reporting.

“These proposals keep checks in place for the most important roles, meaning individuals are accountable for their actions, but reduce the administrative burden where it isn’t needed, giving firms more time to invest in growth-focused activities and greater flexibility in onboarding senior talent,” said Braddick, who was an executive at Barclays plc until earlier this year.

In total, companies will need to spend 53% less on complying with the regime, according to estimates in the consultation paper. The rules were introduced in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis to ensure executives at financial-services firms can be held to account for misconduct that occurs on their watch.

See also: Farage challenger faces £37,000 bill after losing court case

Lawmakers have been looking to narrow the scope of the rules for several years, with Conservative ministers announcing a review as part of the post-Brexit overhaul known as the Edinburgh reforms in 2022.

Regulators signalled last year that they would be streamlining the rules, as part of efforts by Keir Starmer’s Labour government to reduce regulation and spur much-needed economic growth. A consultation on the latest plans will now run until Jan 22.

“Firms will remain responsible for ensuring their employees remain competent, suitable and meet appropriate standards of conduct, and those no longer requiring pre-approval will continue to be held to the same level of accountability as before,” the regulators said in a joint statement.

See also: UK said to raise taxes on banks in budget this month

In a speech at London’s Mansion House, Braddick also said the PRA will create a new directorate to focus on firms’ operational and cyber resilience. The strength of companies’ technology systems is under increasing scrutiny after a spate of cyber attacks spanning from crypto wallets to fridges.

title: Singapore allocates $100 million to subsidise up to 75% of business-led R&D in decarbonisation
article:
Businesses in Singapore can now tap a $100 million fund to spearhead and co-develop technologies that address the city-state's specific industrial decarbonisation challenges, announced deputy prime minister Gan Kim Yong today at the inaugural Singapore Industry Decarbonisation Forum.

The government will co-fund up to 75% of qualifying project costs under the Decarbonisation Research for Industry, Ventures, and Enterprise programme, or DRIVE. Companies, including start-ups and technology providers, can initiate and design R&D projects in partnership with Singapore’s public research institutions to address industry decarbonisation challenges.

The new programme will provide a source of funding to firms that lack capital to conduct research, while helping those with the capital to save costs, potentially catalysing innovation, enhancing business resiliency and boosting bottomlines.

“Under DRIVE, companies will take the lead in defining the decarbonisation challenges they want solved," says Gan. “They can also tap on Singapore’s deep research capabilities to co-develop solutions, with DRIVE co-sharing the R&D investment to take promising ideas further.”

DRIVE is part of a broader $143 million industry decarbonisation funding initiative led by the Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) and the Advanced Energy and Decarbonisation Office (AEDO). Opened to applications, this funding initiative focuses on carbon capture, carbon utilisation and other novel and emerging decarbonisation technologies.

With Singapore’s land and resource constraints limiting the feasibility of deploying some decarbonisation technologies at scale, such targeted R&D to develop bespoke solutions for the city-state is required, according to EDB and AEDO.

See also: Keppel, Sembcorp Industries and Tuas Power roped into Southeast Asia’s first biomethane sandbox

The two entities add that Industrial activities, including manufacturing, account for nearly two-thirds of Singapore’s emissions, making industrial decarbonisation “critical” to achieving the country’s climate goals. However, emissions from energy-intensive activities, such as petrochemical production, refining, and fuel combustion, remain difficult to reduce.

“Manufacturing is a key pillar of our economy, contributing around 20 per cent of GDP and employing one-eighth of our workforce,” remarks Gan. “As we move towards a low-carbon future, we must help our industries make the transition smoothly and successfully, so that they can continue growing and providing good jobs.”

The funding initiative announced today is part of the $800 million Decarbonisation Grand Challenge (DGC), which was announced under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) 2030 Plan earlier this year. The DGC supports promising technologies across the innovation journey – from research and development, to translation, scale-up and demonstration.

See also: Bank of Singapore augments CIO with new sustainability advisory team

“To achieve lower emissions through these investments, we must work closely with industry to develop solutions that meet its needs, prove that these can be scaled, and enable companies to deploy them,” adds Gan.

The new funding initiative will sharpen Singapore’s R&D efforts to develop a pipeline of promising technologies for subsequent scale-up, through programmes such as the Low-Carbon Technology Translational Testbed (LCT3) and Singapore Pilots for Energy & Enterprise Decarbonisation (SPEED). It builds on the earlier Low Carbon Energy Research (LCER) programmes, which have supported R&D in carbon capture, utilisation, and storage, and hydrogen technologies.

It was also announced that AEDO has awarded a total of S$65 million through its LCER Scale-up Grant to five projects which had delivered promising outcomes under an earlier LCER programme. The selected projects include partnerships between: Chevron, YTL PowerSeraya and the National University of Singapore (NUS); Cora Environment and Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR); and PacificLight Power, Siemens, and NUS.

In addition to funding, Gan also announced new partnerships between EDB and AEDO with clean energy investors and accelerators which aim to accelerate technological development, from research to commercialisation. The new partnerships and collaborations are with Extantia, Main Sequence, and Rocky Mountain Institute, building on ongoing collaborations with Breakthrough Energy, Energy Impact Partners, SG Growth Capital, and Temasek.

These partnerships and collaborations will provide global perspectives on emerging technologies and industry needs to inform Singapore’s R&D funding priorities, as well as availing their networks and recommending relevant companies to tap on Singapore’s decarbonisation initiatives. Promising companies can access opportunities for R&D support, develop capabilities around low-carbon technologies, and scale potential solutions for eventual commercial deployment.

Gan also officiated the ground-breaking of the $62.5 million Low-Carbon Technology Translational Testbed (LCT3) at the SIDF. The LCT3 is a national facility that will help companies test and scale emerging low-carbon technologies for industrial use.

Located on Jurong Island and hosted at the A*STAR Institute of Sustainability for Chemicals, Energy and Environment (A*STAR ISCE2), LCT3 will provide modular and configurable facilities to support the development and testing of carbon utilisation and hydrogen technologies under industry-relevant conditions.

Firms can access shared infrastructure, utilities, permits and licences to set up pilots, moving faster from technology development to testing and scale-up. Amogy, IHI Corporation, and Metha8 were announced as LCT3’s first users, through collaborations spanning carbon utilisation and low-carbon hydrogen.

title: OpenAI shifts value to US$1.25 tril as funding talks finalise — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 23): OpenAI, which is seeking to raise around US$30 billion in a fresh funding round, is now targeting a valuation of US$1.25 trillion during the final stages of negotiations, according to people familiar with the matter.

The ChatGPT maker shifted the value discussed in the talks by US$150 billion, from US$1.4 trillion, according to people involved with the talks who asked for anonymity while discussing private details. The fundraising discussions are ongoing and details could change, said the people.

OpenAI most recently raised a US$122 billion round in March at an US$852 billion valuation, including the money.

Coatue Management is in talks to co-lead in the round, according to the people. OpenAI has also been in talks with multiple investment funds from the United Arab Emirates, among other firms including BlackRock Inc., Bloomberg previously reported.

OpenAI declined to comment. Coatue did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The company expects to have commitments from investors finalised by the end of next week, one person said.

See also: Tesla’s lowered capex target fuels doubt on AI, robotics goals

Technology stocks have fallen this week after mixed quarterly earnings results from companies including Meta Platforms Inc and Tesla Inc fuelled investor concerns that massive spending on artificial intelligence has gone too far. Many investors are closely watching how OpenAI rival Anthropic PBC’s initial public offering, which is expected next month, will be received.

OpenAI has pushed back its plans for an initial public offering until next year, citing its focus on AI safety efforts.

title: Keppel, Sembcorp Industries and Tuas Power roped into Southeast Asia’s first biomethane sandbox
article:
The Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) has appointed three generation companies as biomethane aggregators under Singapore’s 300MW regulatory sandbox to import and supply biomethane, a renewable alternative to natural gas. The announcement was made by deputy prime minister Gan Kim Yong at the inaugural Singapore Industry Decarbonisation Forum today.

Keppel’s infrastructure division, Sembcorp’s subsidiary Sembcorp Utilities and Tuas Power will support the testing of commercial, regulatory and operational arrangements needed for biomethane imports, helping to shape the frameworks for the wider adoption of biomethane under the sandbox, the first of its kind in Southeast Asia.

The sandbox will run for 15 years, with the power generators expected to bring in their first biomethane supplies by end-2028, importing biomethane of up to 300MW from regional and international sources to power data centres and industrial manufacturers in Singapore, either as biomethane gas or as biomethane-derived electricity.

Biomethane is a renewable, low-carbon gas produced by upgrading biogas from organic waste sources such as food waste, agricultural residue, animal manure and sewage sludge. This process yields a gas that is chemically identical to fossil-derived methane — the main component of natural gas.

Unlike many emerging low-carbon fuels, biomethane is a direct drop-in replacement for fossil natural gas, as it can utilise existing gas infrastructure and be consumed without modifications to equipment or industrial processes. This makes it one of the most practical near-term decarbonisation options available.

With natural gas accounting for around 95% of Singapore’s electricity generation, biomethane offers a feasible pathway to reduce emissions from the power sector and heavily gas-dependent industries, according to the EDB.

See also: Singapore allocates $100 million to subsidise up to 75% of business-led R&D in decarbonisation

“This biomethane regulatory sandbox is an important pilot to help Singapore discover new decarbonisation pathways for our manufacturing and data centre sectors,” says EDB executive vice president Lim Wey-Len. “By working with our appointed generation companies and industry partners, we aim to establish a credible and sustainable biomethane ecosystem, and build the capabilities needed to support its wider adoption over time.”

Janice Bong, managing director of integrated power business under Keppel’s infrastructure division says that her company’s” integrated” energy capabilities and experience in natural gas sourcing and procurement as well as cross-border power importation provide a “strong” foundation to help develop Singapore’s biomethane pathway. “By consolidating demand for biomethane, we can achieve economies of scale and optimise costs, enabling wider adoption and decarbonisation across multiple sectors," she adds.

Koh Chiap Khiong, CEO of Sembcorp’s gas and related services business, believes that Sembcorp is” well positioned” to both support the development of Singapore’s biomethane value chain and adoption of the emerging fuel. “In doing so, we can contribute to Singapore’s energy transition and help meet growing power demand from an increasingly digital and AI-driven economy,” he adds.

Ida Handojo, senior vice president for fuel management at Tuas Power, says that her company’s experience in the Southeast Asian biomass market and logistic handling can support Singapore’s journey to develop the use of biomethane at scale. “With more than 90% of Singapore’s power generation currently coming from natural gas-fired CCGTs, biomethane can be a potential solution to meet our decarbonisation targets and the growing demand from companies for cleaner energy,” she adds.

title: Beng Kuang Marine unlocks shareholder value with new asset-light, service-centric model serving offshore and marine
article:
In the decade from 2013 to 2022, Mainboard-listed Beng Kuang Marine suffered cumulative losses attributable to shareholders of more than $71 million. During this period, the company’s business was split into four segments, namely infrastructure engineering (IE), corrosion prevention (CP), supply and distribution, as well as shipping and others.

Established in the 1990s as a subcontractor providing corrosion prevention services to shipyards, Beng Kuang has since grown progressively to diversify into various aspects of the offshore and marine (O&M) industries.

The downturn of the offshore and marine industry from mid-2014 onwards impacted its performance for several years, and a key contributor to the losses was the shipping division, which was unable to contribute profit as shipping assets were under-utilised due to third-party operating issues, excessive downtime for repairs and cost challenges, says CEO Yong Jiunn Run. Following three straight years of losses, the Singapore Exchange (SGX) placed Beng Kuang on its watchlist in mid-2023.

After he joined the company in mid-2021, Yong set out to turn around the business and return it to profitability, which was achieved in FY2023. Today, after exiting the SGX watchlist in Oct 2024, Beng Kuang is firmly in the black with a net cash position and positioned for its next phase of growth.

Reporting positive earnings from FY2023 to FY2025 and peaking at $11.5 million for FY2024, Beng Kuang has continued its strong momentum into 2026. For the first half of this year, it reported close to 21% y-o-y growth in patmi to $3.5 million, with revenue of $55.7 million, which is around 10% y-o-y higher. It has also updated that its order book stood at around $71.5 million as at end-September. The current situation stands in contrast to FY2022, when the company reported its highest-ever loss of $21.8 million.

See also: SIA Engineering finds itself on firmer footing post-Covid

With more than three decades of experience in corporate banking, Yong was brought in and charged with charting Beng Kuang’s strategic direction. Under his watch, the company has monetised its non-core fixed assets, hived off underperforming segments and focused on high-potential business segments to create new growth catalysts.

Under the Beng Kuang 2.0 roadmap, Yong narrowed the group’s focus to the “high-growth, cash-generative” IE and CP services segments, transforming into an asset-light and service-centric model which contrasts with its asset-heavy past, which incurred high capex and depreciation.

Together, these two divisions provide specialised engineering, maintenance and regulatory compliance solutions that support the reliability, safety and longevity of marine and offshore assets across the energy value chain.

See also: Cosco readies for growth as efficient, reliable, end-to-end logistics provider in Southeast Asia

This has enabled Beng Kuang to enhance the quality of its earnings, from lumpy contracts to more stable recurring income streams. “The main motive for the transformation is to create high-quality recurring income streams, in addition to better controlling costs,” says Yong. “Previously, earnings were cyclical and dependent on ‘lumpy’ contracts, but now, we do not have to live from contract to contract.”

On a segmental basis, the IE division contributed $19.7 million in operating profit on $78.5 million in revenue for FY2025 ended Dec 31, while the CP division reported $19.6 million revenue, with operating profit of $2.3 million.

The main driver behind Beng Kuang’s brighter prospects is its subsidiary, Asian Sealand Offshore and Marine (ASOM), which became wholly-owned by Beng Kuang in May after Beng Kuang acquired the remaining 49% stake following shareholders’ approval.

In FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025, ASOM reported profits after tax of $10 million, $19.3 million and $14.9 million respectively, on revenue of $50.6 million, $86.3 million and $75.2 million respectively. The bulk of Beng Kuang’s earnings from the IE division is derived from ASOM.

ASOM was incubated by Beng Kuang in 2016, reveals Yong. He adds that by making ASOM a wholly-owned subsidiary, Beng Kuang has strengthened operational alignment across the group’s business, offering greater strategic flexibility in supporting offshore energy clients across multiple markets.

The main business of ASOM is to provide asset integrity solutions for floating, production, storage and offloading (FPSO) and floating, storage and offloading (FSO) vessels, which are typically anchored to their production site for their entire lifecycle, operating 24/7, regardless of oil prices. ASOM has established itself as a proficient “one-stop” in-situ turnkey solutions provider, spanning maintenance, repairs, installation, commissioning, operations and decommissioning for the vessels.
